non-being-that-is-there, which underlies real human existence.

There is also a fourth combination that is formally possible: non-being-that-is-not-there. But there is nothing to say about this. It is pure non-being or nothingness, which is, so to speak, completely filled by being in its other three aspects.

It is like the canvas behind a painting when every part of the canvas has been covered by paint, or like darkness penetrated everywhere by light. In other words, it is what Plato called “matter”: something that is not, and about which nothing can therefore be said.
Ontology consequently has three fundamental parts.
Cosmology, by contrast, has only two.
Contrary to Plato, ideal being does not exist independently. The same is admittedly true of human being, which cannot exist without natural being. But natural being can exist without human being.
We therefore obtain two types of existence and two fundamental parts of Cosmology:
the doctrine of the natural world;
the doctrine of the human or historical world.
The human world itself divides into three “worlds.” None can exist without human beings, and human beings cannot exist without them:
the technical world created by human work;
the sociopolitical world created by human struggle;
the “ideal” world created by human speech or discourse.
This last world is, in Marx’s expression, a “superstructure” erected above the technical and political world, which in turn has the natural world as its real foundation.
The structure of Phenomenology will be discussed in the final chapter of this introduction.

162) Suppose the botanist and the physicist describe the same object—a birch tree.

The botanist uses everything given directly in ordinary sense perception. The physicist, by contrast, relates that perception to an “idealized eye” which “sees” not a birch tree but the electrons, protons, electromagnetic waves, and so on that compose it—even though none of these things is given in ordinary sense perception.
The physicist forgets this, however, and concludes that the “real” birch tree is not the green tree with a white trunk described by the botanist, but this system of electrons.

The botanist, on the other hand—unless he has been intimidated by the prestige of mathematical physics—is inclined to treat the physicist’s system as an “abstraction” and to regard his own birch tree as the “real” one.
In fact, both birch trees are abstractions.
Only the birch tree that includes both its “botanical” aspect and its “physical” aspect, along with many others, is concrete.
It is therefore Cosmology that studies this concrete birch tree—or, if not the tree itself, then the world in which such a tree can grow and become an object of study for both botanist and physicist.

163) Everything said here will apply fully only to the definitive Phenomenology, which will be written in communist society. In that society every individual—and a fortiori its author—will have been freed from national and social limitations and from every form of one-sidedness, and will therefore appear simply as a “human being as such.”

As for “personal” limitations, everyone has to free themselves from those individually. But in principle this can happen in any society. In pre-communist society one can project oneself into a class or a nation, and in communist society into humanity as a whole.
There will admittedly still be dependence on unconscious “instincts,” above all sexual instincts. But here, at least in principle, Freud’s psychoanalysis can serve as a corrective.
My own Phenomenology, however, is being written in a socialist society and is therefore, in a sense, that society’s ideology.
Yet my Phenomenology differs fundamentally from “science” because it knows this and says so.
“Science” does not know that it is an “ideology.”
Pre-communist Phenomenology knows that it is an ideology.
Communist Phenomenology knows itself as knowledge.
164) I am referring only to that part of Phenomenology which describes how human consciousness knows the natural world.

Phenomenology as a whole, however, describes the entire content of human consciousness. From it we will therefore come to know the human being as a whole, not merely the human being insofar as he knows nature.

But, as we will now see, Phenomenology does not describe what the human being actually is. That is the subject of the second part of Cosmology. Phenomenology describes how human beings “appear” to themselves.

Yet a human being’s “appearance” to himself—that is, self-consciousness—is itself, in a certain sense, part of what the human being is. Phenomenology is therefore, after all, also a science of the human being himself.

Phenomenological anthropology differs from cosmological anthropology only in this respect: the former confines itself to describing human self-consciousness, whereas the latter investigates human beings in their real existence within the natural world.

If one prefers, cosmological anthropology studies the relation between consciousness and the human being as a whole, and through the human being the relation between consciousness and the natural or material world as a whole.
165) Even when a psychologist uses “introspection,” he does not usually ask how or why he is able to observe himself.
In any case, he is not interested in the person who is observing himself—that is, in himself as a human being living under particular natural and historical conditions.
While observing “himself,” he simultaneously forgets himself, just as the scientist and the ordinary observer forget themselves while looking at a birch tree.
166) Suppose the object of Phenomenology is a particular “sense perception.” Phenomenology will still describe:
what this “perception” seems to be to the human being who has it, whether an ordinary person, a psychologist, or someone else;
how that person recognizes and understands this “perception”;
what kind of consciousness possesses and recognizes this “perception,” and thereby presents itself as self-consciousness.
Historically, this self-consciousness—and therefore consciousness itself—changes, or more exactly creates history. As it changes, cognition changes with it.
What “appears” through this cognition therefore changes too: what human beings think and in general “know” about sense perception.
But the concept itself—that is, perception as studied by the cosmologist—remains unchanged in itself, although it too, of course, appeared in time like everything human and will one day disappear.
The psychologist, by contrast, wrongly assumes that the perception he is talking about does not change. In other words, he wrongly assumes that the “appearance of sense perception” does not change.
167) Phenomenology will admittedly not talk about itself in the chapter where it discusses the Roman Empire.

But in that chapter it will also discuss the kind of “cognition” through which the Roman Empire “appears.” And Phenomenology as a whole will ultimately include both the discourse about itself and the discourse about that cognition.

Phenomenology will obviously not describe every single “appearance” of the Roman Empire—for example, every detail of its historical development. Instead, it will describe all the general possible points of view, thereby allowing the reader to “deduce” every possible historical viewpoint, including viewpoints on the Roman Empire.

As we will see, when Phenomenology describes a given “appearance,” it does not describe the cognition and consciousness attached to that appearance, but those attached to the next appearance. We will understand the reason for this later.

What matters here is that this “flight forward” does nothing to undermine the exhaustiveness of the description. In the end, all phenomena will have been described, together with all forms of “consciousness” and all forms of “cognition.”
168) Plato’s philosophy does, of course, speak about these things itself. An historian explaining Plato’s philosophy will therefore also mention them.
But it is still Plato who is philosophizing, not the historian.

Whenever an historian presents a philosophy, the content he presents will naturally be philosophical. But ordinary history itself has nothing to do with philosophy. It describes philosophy in the same way that an historian might describe the art of war or a botanist might describe a birch tree.
169) This is why the best name for Phenomenology remains simply “Phenomenology.”
The word “dialectic” captures its philosophical character, but not what makes it specifically phenomenological.

It is perfectly correct to define Phenomenology as a “phenomenological and dialectical anthropology.” But this is obviously not much of a definition, since the word that needs defining appears inside the definition itself.

My own “socialist” Phenomenology does not yet end in complete self-consciousness. It nevertheless ends in a form of self-consciousness that cannot be surpassed under the existing historical conditions.

A Phenomenology that is not yet definitive cannot describe all “appearances,” but only those that have actually occurred before its own appearance.

174) “Scholarly” history, insofar as it is more than a simple chronicle, also looks for laws of historical development.

Some historians deny this, claiming that history merely describes “historical phenomena” without looking for their “causes.” But everyone agrees that there is some science which does look for those causes: the discipline that, since Auguste Comte, has been called “sociology.”
To avoid pointless arguments, we can therefore apply what follows to sociology rather than to history.

Because the historian deals with abstractions, the “historical” law he discovers resembles the “scientific” laws of the natural world. It therefore differs fundamentally from a philosophical or “dialectical” law.
The difference is precisely that such a law applies only to historical “reality” separated from the experience or consciousness corresponding to it.

It goes without saying that these abstractions—and the laws governing these abstractions, meaning “phenomena” or concepts taken by themselves—are not dialectical. The same is true of the laws of psychology.
Neither “reality” by itself nor “consciousness” by itself is dialectical.
What is dialectical is reality that has become conscious of itself: human existence taken as a whole, which is what Phenomenology studies.

As for “Marxist,” that is, dialectical, history, it belongs—like Hegel’s “history,” from which it derives—to philosophy, not to “science” in the ordinary sense. More precisely, it belongs to Cosmology.

Marxist philosophy and economics differ from phenomenological “history” because Marx deals with existence itself, whereas Phenomenology deals with that existence in its secondary form as “appearance.”
This amounts to saying that Phenomenology abstracts from the natural world in which historical processes occur, whereas “Marxism” relates those processes to that world. See note 163.
